output.brief: The Admissions Office does not appear to be the main reason enrolment fell. Applications and admits both rose, so the applicant pool isn't the problem. Yield (the share of admits who enrolled) fell from 41.8% to 34.3%. That drop is concentrated in the two scholarship tiers whose awards were cut: Dean's, from $14,000 to $9,000, fell from 45.2% to 31.9%. Merit, from $9,000 to $5,000, fell from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards were unchanged and yield held at about 36%. Admits with no merit award held at roughly 37%. Early-action admits, who were decided on the old system and on time, saw yield fall almost as much (45.2% to 37.8%) as regular-decision admits (39.0% to 31.5%). So portal delays don't explain most of the loss. The finance committee's low price-sensitivity assumption looks wrong. I'm fairly confident, though not certain. The data doesn't split the tiers by round, and the delays may have cost some students. Next steps: don't replace the director on this evidence. Take the award schedule back to the finance committee with a modelled proposal to restore the cut tiers. Set a turnaround target for regular decisions. Check the missing-transcript complaints before ordering a vendor rebuild.
